stage_description: Adolescence runs from about three to six months and is a time of fast growth and rising hormones. Rabbits become more energetic, territorial, and sometimes challenging: chewing, digging, mounting, boxing with the front paws, and litter-box lapses are all typical as sexual maturity arrives (often earlier in small breeds). This is a normal, temporary phase. Patient handling and, in due course, spaying or neutering help settle the behaviour and prevent unwanted litters and reproductive disease.
nutrition: Growth is still rapid, so young rabbits stay on unlimited alfalfa hay and unlimited pellets through this stage, always with unlimited fresh water. From around twelve weeks begin introducing fresh leafy greens one type at a time in small amounts, watching the droppings for any softening. Keep starchy or sugary treats to a minimum while the gut is still settling into an adult diet.
activity: Energy peaks now, so give several hours a day out of the enclosure, in a space cleared of cables and hazards, to run, jump, and explore. Channel natural urges with digging boxes, cardboard tunnels, willow chews, and foraging toys, and protect wires and furniture from busy teeth. Plenty of appropriate outlets reduces destructive chewing and keeps a lively adolescent content.
veterinary_check_frequency: This is the key stage to plan spaying or neutering with a rabbit-savvy vet: it curbs hormonal behaviour, prevents litters, and greatly lowers the risk of uterine cancer in females. Use the pre-surgery visit for a full check of teeth, weight, and body condition. Otherwise a healthy adolescent needs only a routine exam roughly once during this period unless problems appear.
dental_care: Continuously growing teeth still depend on constant grinding against hay, so hay must remain the bulk of the diet even as greens are added. Offer safe wooden and willow chews to satisfy the urge to gnaw, and watch for weight loss, drooling, or dropped food that could point to malocclusion needing veterinary attention.
warning_signs: Any refusal to eat, or no droppings for more than about twelve hours, is a gut-stasis emergency, so see a rabbit-savvy vet at once. Act quickly too on diarrhea, a bloated or painful belly, a hunched posture with teeth-grinding, a head tilt, or laboured breathing. Sudden aggression or straining without droppings can likewise signal illness rather than simple adolescence.
source_name: House Rabbit Society & Oxbow Rabbit Life Stages
disclaimer: This information is for educational purposes only and does not replace consultation with a veterinarian.
